entry.title: OpenCode on Your Phone: Remote Sessions with Tailscale and the Web App as a PWA
entry.summary: OpenCode has no mobile app, and it doesn't need one: the server already running on your desktop serves its own web UI, and that UI installs as a PWA. This is how I reach it from my phone over Tailscale, with HTTPS and nothing exposed to the internet.
entry.content:
When I leave a long session working on my desktop, what I want is to check on it from the sofa. It turns out that doesn't require installing any app on the phone: OpenCode already serves its own web interface from the same server the TUI and the desktop app use. You just have to make the phone able to reach that server.

I set it up with Tailscale and the web app installed as a PWA: no public tunnels and not a single port opened on the router.

Client and server, that's the whole thing¶

Since version 2, OpenCode is client/server. There's a background service holding the sessions, the files, the providers and the credentials, and then there are clients that talk to it: the TUI, the desktop app and the web. The desktop app, in fact, starts that same service when you open it.

Which means a "remote session" isn't a separate feature: it's just another client connecting to the server you already have running. You can see it with:

opencode service status
# http://127.0.0.1:49374

The default port depends on the platform: 49374 on macOS, Linux and WSL, and 28894 on Windows (Windows reserves the high ports, and WSL with mirrored networking takes a block too). By default it listens on localhost only and asks for a password, which is generated on first start.

How pairing works by default¶

The native mechanism is opencode pair. It prints a one-time link and a QR code:

opencode pair

# Open a link to connect. Links work once and expire in 5 minutes.
# http://127.0.0.1:49374/auth/connect/...

Opening that link in a browser signs you in with a cookie and loads the web UI. The session lasts 30 days, and changing the server password revokes all of them. In the desktop app the same thing lives under Settings → Pairing → Pair device, which shows the QR code to scan from another device.

To leave localhost there are two paths, and this is the important decision:

The official path: OpenTunnel. opencode pair --remote brings up an end-to-end encrypted tunnel to a public relay and gives you an HTTPS address reachable from anywhere. The first time it warns that it's about to expose the server to the internet and asks for confirmation. You still need the password, but the server now has a door on the internet. It's exactly what the desktop's Pair device button does: it turns on opencode service set remote true and builds the QR from the tunnel's public URL (to switch it off, opencode service set remote false).

Your own path: your private network. If Tailscale is already on your devices, the phone and the desktop can see each other over a private IP without exposing anything. That's the one I use.

Tailscale instead of OpenTunnel¶

The piece that makes this comfortable is tailscale serve. It keeps OpenCode listening on localhost and lets Tailscale terminate TLS and publish that port inside the tailnet. First you need MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates enabled in the Tailscale admin console; without certificates, Serve can't give you HTTPS.

tailscale serve --bg 49374
tailscale serve status
# https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net

And now you generate the pairing link with the external URL, not with localhost:

opencode pair --url https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net

That link already carries the right host, so it works both for pasting it on the phone and for scanning the QR. The server keeps listening on 127.0.0.1 only: no need to touch hostname 0.0.0.0 or open ports on your router. To undo it, tailscale serve reset.

One practical detail: since Pair device is already wired to OpenTunnel, using Tailscale means going through the CLI. Leave Remote access off in the settings and use opencode pair --url, which talks to the same background service.

Installing it as a PWA¶

You open the link in the phone's browser and it just works. To stop it feeling like a tab, Chrome's menu offers Install app (or Add to Home screen). It's not a shortcut: the web interface ships a manifest with display: standalone, 192 and 512 icons, an apple-touch-icon and a Workbox service worker that precaches the application shell. Opening it from the icon gives you no address bar and no tabs.

This is why HTTPS matters. Installing a PWA and using the camera to scan the QR are secure context features: they work on https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net, while on http://100.x.y.z:49374 the browser only lets you browse. Done this way, the phone gets its own icon, full screen and a camera for the QR.

The service worker caches the shell: lose coverage and the app still opens with no server behind it. There's no magic though, sessions still live on the desktop, so without a network you get an empty shell with no data.

What you can do from the phone¶

The web app is the same application as the desktop one, not a cut-down version. From the phone I can:

  • Watch the conversation live, with reasoning, tools and per-turn diffs.
  • Approve or deny permissions, which is 90% of what I need when I'm away.
  • Open the integrated terminal, with an on-screen keyboard and the control keys at hand.
  • Browse project files, including PDFs and Office documents.
  • Switch model, agent and reasoning level.

What I wouldn't expect from it:

  • No push notifications. The browser notification only fires while the page is open or hidden; if the system freezes the tab, the SSE stream dies and nothing arrives.
  • Typing long prompts on a phone is still punishment, however good dictation is.
  • The desktop has to be on and the service alive. Turn it off and there's no session to look at.

Security in four lines¶

  • The server password is still mandatory; Tailscale protects the network, not the application.
  • Restrict access in the tailnet with ACLs or Grants to machine:443 for your devices.
  • Don't enable Funnel. Serve is for your tailnet; Funnel publishes the service to the internet, and then you're back to OpenTunnel but without its end-to-end encryption.
  • If you ever get suspicious, change the password with opencode service set password "...": every 30-day session drops at once.

Alternatives¶

If you'd rather not set up Serve, ssh -L does the same for a local client:

ssh -L 49374:127.0.0.1:49374 my-server

And inside the tailnet, without certificates, opencode service set hostname 0.0.0.0 plus http://100.x.y.z:49374 also works. Traffic is still encrypted by WireGuard, but since it isn't a secure context you lose PWA installation and the camera. Fine for a one-off; for daily use, Serve is much better.

Wrapping up¶

OpenCode's remote sessions aren't a separate product, they're a consequence of everything being client/server: the server is already on your desktop, and all you need is a client that can reach it. The web UI it serves is the full app, and with Tailscale Serve you get real HTTPS without exposing anything. It's the cleanest way I've found to follow a session from my phone without installing anything weird.

Source: OpenCode — Web, OpenCode — Commands and Tailscale Serve.

entry.title: rbw-env: Export environment variables from Bitwarden
entry.summary: Using rbw to export environment variables from Bitwarden, useful for setting API keys securely without storing them on disk.
entry.content:
Continuing the kitty-rbw saga, today I present another script from the same project: rbw-env.

The problem¶

I use pi-agent with different AI models (Claude, OpenAI, Gemini...) and each requires its own API_KEY. Keeping these keys on disk is a security risk, and having to enter them every time is tedious.

The solution: rbw-env¶

The script exports Bitwarden entries as environment variables. The idea is simple but effective:

  1. Select a folder with fzf (e.g., "ai-providers")
  2. rbw-env exports each entry as export VARIABLE='value'
  3. The temp file deletes itself after sourcing

Usage¶

# Interactive folder selection
kitty @ kitten kitty_rbw/rbw_env.py

# Or pass folder as argument
kitty @ kitten kitty_rbw/rbw_env.py ai-providers

The command creates a temporary file in /tmp/kitty_rbw_env_* and sends the source command to the window:

source /tmp/kitty_rbw_env_qfdhyh_b

The last line of the temp file is the deletion of the file itself:

rm -f /tmp/kitty_rbw_env_qfdhyh_b

Bitwarden structure¶

Each entry in the exported folder uses:

  • Username: variable name (e.g., ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
  • Password: variable value (e.g., sk-ant-...)
  • Name: optional description

If any entry has username or name equal to NOEXPORT, it's skipped (useful for notes).

Integration with kitty-rbw¶

In the previous post I explained how to install kitty-rbw. With Ctrl+Alt+Shift+b I get the folder selector to export environment variables.

entry.title: Tailscale Aperture: AI Gateway Without Distributing API Keys
entry.summary: Tailscale's Aperture centralizes LLM access by eliminating the need to distribute API keys to developers, using Tailscale identity for authentication.
entry.content:
One thing that kept me up at night when I started using LLMs at work was: where do I store the API keys? In private repos, in .env files I forgot to gitignore, in phone notes... A mess.

Tailscale recently announced Aperture, an AI gateway that runs inside your tailnet and completely eliminates that problem.

The Problem with Distributed API Keys¶

When developers need access to OpenAI, Anthropic, or any other LLM provider, the common practice has been:

  1. Create an API key
  2. Share it via Slack, email, or pasted in a private repo
  3. Pray it doesn't leak
  4. When someone leaves, manually rotate all keys

This doesn't scale. An organization with 50 developers can have hundreds of keys floating around in documents, CI/CD scripts, and developer machines that are no longer at the company.

Aperture: Centralization with Real Identity¶

Tailscale's solution is elegant: use tailnet identity for authentication, not distributed keys.

How it works:

  1. Configure Aperture in your tailnet with your provider API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter, etc.)
  2. Developers connect to Aperture using their Tailscale identity
  3. Aperture injects the credentials for the corresponding provider and forwards the request
  4. Complete telemetry: tokens used, costs, sessions, all in a dashboard

Developers never see the real API keys. Aperture keeps them centralized and injects them server-side.

Integration with Existing Tools¶

The good news is it works with the tools you already use:

  • Claude Code: Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://ai and you're done
  • Codex: Base URL to Aperture
  • Gemini CLI, Roo Code, Cline: Similar, change the base URL
  • Custom apps: Works with any client using OpenAI-compatible APIs

From the client's perspective, Aperture looks like the provider itself. It detects the model in the request body and routes to the correct provider.

pi-ts-aperture: Plugin for Pi¶

There's an official Pi plugin to automatically route through Aperture:

pi install npm:@aliou/pi-ts-aperture
/aperture:setup

The wizard asks for: 1. Your Aperture URL (e.g., ai.your-tailnet.ts.net) 2. Which providers to route

It saves configuration to ~/.pi/agent/extensions/aperture.json and modifies providers to use Aperture as proxy.

Visibility and Control¶

Aperture'sdashboard gives you:

  • Tokens by model and user: How much does each person spend?
  • Grouped sessions: A Claude Code session can have50 requests; you see them as a coherent unit
  • Tool use: Which tools are being invoked and how frequently
  • Adoption: Who's using what, and who tried once and didn't come back
  • Export to S3: To integrate with your usual SIEM

For platform or security teams that need auditing, this is gold.

Requirements¶

  • A Tailscale tailnet (fundamental, all authentication depends on Tailscale identity)
  • API keys for the providers you want to use
  • The device running Pi must be on the tailnet

In Summary¶

If your organization is adopting AI tools and you don't want to deal with API keys circulating everywhere, Aperture is a clean solution. It centralizes credentials, gives real visibility into usage, and uses the identity infrastructure you already have with Tailscale.

It's still in alpha, but available for free during the testing period. Worth trying if you already use Tailscale.

entry.title: rbw: The Bitwarden terminal client you should be using
entry.summary: How to install and configure rbw, a Rust implementation of the Bitwarden client, and how to integrate it into your workflows with pi-agent.
entry.content:
While Bitwarden has an official command-line client, it can be slow as it is Node.js-based. For those of us looking for something more agile, rbw is the ideal solution. It is an unofficial Rust implementation that stands out for being extremely fast and for managing vault unlocking through an agent, preventing you from having to enter your master password for every command.

Installation¶

The easiest way to install it is by downloading the binary directly from its GitHub releases. I use gah for this purpose:

gah install doy/rbw

This command will download the rbw binary and the rbw-agent binary.

Initial Setup¶

The first thing is to configure your account and the server:

rbw login

It will ask for your email and the server URL (you can leave it blank if you use the official Bitwarden one or enter the URL of your Vaultwarden instance).

To start using it, unlock the vault:

rbw unlock

Unlike the official client, you don't need to export environment variables with session tokens. The rbw agent takes care of everything in the background.

Basic Usage¶

To get a password quickly:

rbw get "Item Name"

If there are multiple items with the same name, you can use filters or the ID. You can also get custom fields or the username:

rbw get "OpenRouter" --folder "APIs"
rbw get --username "Twitter"

Integration with pi-agent¶

One of the greatest advantages of having a fast and secure CLI client is the ability to integrate secrets into your development tools.

pi-agent allows executing commands to obtain API keys dynamically. This avoids having to save keys in plain text configuration files. In your settings.json, you can configure access to a key as follows:

{ 
    "type": "api_key", 
    "key": "!rbw get 'OpenRouter'" 
}

The ! prefix tells pi-agent to execute the command and use its standard output as the key. Thanks to the rbw agent, this command will run instantly without asking for your master password every time, as long as the vault is unlocked.

entry.title: Sysdig: Cloud-Native Security Platform with AI
entry.summary: Sysdig offers a comprehensive security platform for cloud-native environments that combines AI, real-time visibility, and open source innovation
entry.content:
Sysdig is a cloud security platform that provides comprehensive, real-time security solutions for cloud-native environments, resolving the conflict between the needs of security and development teams.

Key Features¶

Intelligent Security AI¶

  • Contextual AI that understands cloud environments and guides actionable insights
  • 76% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR)

Real-Time Visibility¶

  • Continuous monitoring of cloud activities and potential risks
  • Threat detection in 2 seconds
  • Filters noise to highlight only critical issues

Open Innovation¶

  • Based on open source technologies like Falco
  • Transparency and customization in cloud security

Key Benefits¶

  • 95% savings in vulnerability management time
  • 98% reduction in vulnerability noise
  • Ultra-fast threat detection

Value Proposition¶

Sysdig enables security and development teams to work more effectively, enabling rapid innovation without compromising security. The platform is used by major companies like IBM, Booking.com, and Neo4j to secure their cloud environments.

This tool represents the future of cloud-native security: intelligent, fast, and uncompromising.

Official site: Sysdig
